title: White wine styles
subtitle: Crisp, aromatic and rich
objectives: Describe three broad styles of white wine
Explain how skins are kept out of white wine
Link a white style to climate and winemaking

steps.title: Three ways a white can taste
steps.body: White wines fall into three broad styles. Light and crisp, like Muscadet or Pinot Grigio, with high acidity and little aroma. Aromatic, like Riesling or Gewürztraminer, with intense floral or fruity smells. Full and rich, like oaked Chardonnay, with a weighty, creamy texture.

steps.title: How a white is made
steps.body: For white wine the grapes are pressed quickly and the juice is fermented without the skins, so it picks up almost no colour or tannin. Fermentation is usually cool, around 12 to 18 degrees Celsius, which keeps fresh fruit aromas. Fermenting or ageing in oak barrels, as many Chardonnays are, adds body and notes of vanilla and toast.

steps.prompt: Why does a white wine have almost no tannin?
options: The juice ferments without the skins
steps.explanation: Tannin comes mostly from skins and seeds. White wine juice is separated from them before fermentation, so very little is extracted.

steps.title: Climate shapes the style
steps.body: Cool climates keep acidity high and alcohol moderate, giving crisp whites such as Chablis. Warm climates give riper fruit, more alcohol and a rounder feel, as in many Chardonnays from California or Australia. The same grape can land in different styles depending on where it grows and how it's made.

steps.prompt: Which of these push a white wine towards a fuller, richer style?
steps.explanation: Warmth gives riper fruit and more alcohol, and oak adds texture and flavour. Early picking and cool climates both keep a wine lighter and crisper.

steps.title: What you learned
points: White wines are broadly crisp, aromatic or rich
The juice ferments without skins, so whites have almost no tannin
Cool climates give crisp whites; warmth and oak give richer ones
